demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about why the event has happened to me
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

issues.item: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy items imply an ongoing external danger/escape-monitoring profile more typical of fear-based threat from assault, accident re-exposure, or unsafe environments. That does not fit well with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another,' where the central disturbance is more plausibly guilt, responsibility, and intrusive memory rather than escape positioning.

Mirror checking is not clinically coherent with the rest of this profile. For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another, the other selected items center on dissociative/fragmented memory and guilt-focused rumination/meaning seeking. Mirror checking instead suggests appearance/body/reality checking behavior that is not supported by the memory items, not linked by the formulation's active edges, and is hard to explain as part of the same PTSD presentation here.

vignette: Leilani's eyes still widened in horror when she recalled the sound of crunching metal and shattering glass. It had been six months since the accident, but the memory remained fragmented – like a puzzle with missing pieces. There were parts she simply couldn't remember, no matter how hard she tried. The investigating officer had told her that she'd accidentally caused serious injury to another person while on duty as a security guard, but Leilani's own recollection ended abruptly at the moment of impact. As she struggled to fill in the gaps, Leilani found herself drawn into an endless cycle of self-blame and rumination. She couldn't shake the feeling that there must have been something she could've done differently – some warning sign she'd missed or a decision she'd botched. These thoughts swirled through her mind like a vortex, sucking in every waking moment. Leilani would replay the event over and over, trying to make sense of it all, but each iteration only seemed to raise more questions. The memory itself felt alien, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to her. Sometimes, when she recalled what had happened, Leilani felt completely numb – like a spectator watching a stranger's life unfold on screen. This emotional disconnect only added to her confusion and self-doubt. Why couldn't she remember the details? What was wrong with her? As she wrestled with these questions, Leilani began to overanalyse every aspect of the event. She'd pore over the police report, searching for clues that might explain what had happened. Her mind would snag on minor inconsistencies or ambiguities, which would then balloon into full-blown obsessions. This constant mental revisiting of the accident only served to further entrench her feelings of guilt and inadequacy. Leilani's attempts to make sense of the event – to impose some semblance of order on chaos – ultimately led her back to the same haunted memories. Her recall would falter, and she'd be left staring into the void, unsure what had really occurred. This uncertainty fueled her maladaptive strategies, which in turn kept the memory alive, refusing to let it settle into a coherent narrative. The weight of these fragmented recollections bore down on Leilani like a physical force. As a security guard, she was no longer able to perform her duties with confidence – every patrol felt like a ticking time bomb waiting to unleash another disaster. The anxiety had begun to seep into other areas of her life, too, making it difficult for her to sleep or focus on everyday tasks. What finally brought Leilani to seek help was the dawning realisation that she couldn't keep living in this limbo – trapped between a past she couldn't fully recall and a present she couldn't fully inhabit. She longed to be free from the suffocating grip of self-blame, to somehow reintegrate her memories into a cohesive whole. As she sat in the therapist's office, Leilani knew that she was taking the first tentative steps towards confronting the trauma head-on – and reclaiming control over her own narrative.
